newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland won't protest over eggs thrown at president.
newsitem.headline: Poland won't protest over eggs thrown at president.

text.p: Poland is concerned that its president's security was threatened when four rightist Poles got close enough to fling eggs at him in Paris but will not protest to France, officials said on Monday.
The government's spokeswoman, Aleksandra Jakubowska, said France had failed to provide adequate security for President Aleksander Kwasniewski.
"Judging from the information we have, not everything was done to ensure proper security for the president," she said at a news briefing.
"If eggs could reach (the president), so could...stones, if not hand grenades," she said.
But Poland will not issue a diplomatic protest note although it will ask the French to investigate the incident and discover all the circumstances, Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said.
"This was not an event that would require a diplomatic note on the part of the Polish foreign ministry," he told PAP news agency.
Kwasniewski, a former communist turned social democrat, and his wife Jolanta were entering a Paris theatre to attend a concert on Sunday when attackers threw the eggs.
They missed Kwasniewski, but Polish news media reported that two of his aides were hit and were planning civil lawsuits against their attackers, who were detained by police.
Two small, virtually unknown rightist groups held a news conference to say that their members had travelled to Paris specifically to hurl eggs at Kwasniewski.

"We express solidarity with our colleagues arrested in France and we will stand in their defence using all legal means," PAP news agency quoted the leader of one group, Piotr Lisiewicz, as telling reporters in the western city of Poznan.
Jakubowska said the Polish government would discuss the incident on Tuesday.

Kwasniewski, in office since 1995, and his political allies from the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance, are often heckled during public appearances in Poland by rightists, who say their involvement in the old regime before 1989 should disqualify them from politics.
Mainstream right and centre opposition parties, which hope to defeat the ex-communists in this year's parliamentary elections, mostly distance themselves from such incidents.

Kwasniewski, due to return to Warsaw late on Monday, met his counterpart Jacques Chirac earlier in the day and received fresh confirmation of France's support for Poland's efforts to quickly join NATO and the European Union.
